title: Outworld Labs Builds Robot Simulation Around the Difficulty of Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Outworld Labs Builds Robot Simulation Around the Difficulty of Dexterous Manipulation
body_markdown:
[Outworld Labs](https://outworldlabs.com/) is developing a simulation platform for training and evaluating robot foundation models, with dexterous manipulation at the center of its physics engine. The product, called Horizon, is intended to reduce how much robotics teams must rely on physical hardware and manual data collection.


The company’s launch describes a recurring cost in robot development: an experiment needs more than a model and a computer. It can require a robot, a human operator, a task setup and a reset before the next attempt. Repeating that process across different objects and environments makes data collection and evaluation difficult to scale.


Simulation offers a way to repeat more work in software, but only if its results are useful outside the simulator. Outworld identifies inaccurate physics and limited environment diversity as obstacles to transferring simulated learning to real robots. It also points to the complexity of existing tools for setting up, scaling and debugging those workloads.


[Watch the original launch video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mnklLUU5Bdk)


Horizon is the company’s response to that combination of problems. Its core is a new physics engine designed for dexterous manipulation. Around it, Outworld is building tools for creating realistic environments, reconstructing and augmenting real-world data, and running simulation, training and evaluation jobs within one platform.


The emphasis on manipulation gives the project a more specific starting point than a general-purpose virtual world. The company wants the simulator to support the interactions required for robots to work with objects, while also making it practical for researchers to create and vary the situations those robots encounter.


Outworld describes its goal as generating more diverse training data and evaluating models across tasks, objects and environments. The launch does not report measured improvements in model performance, a quantified reduction in collection costs or a benchmark establishing equivalence with physical experiments. Its ambition should therefore not be treated as an independently demonstrated result.


The platform approach matters because fidelity alone is not the whole workflow. Researchers need to prepare an environment, run jobs, inspect what happened and compare results. Outworld is proposing to bring those steps together, rather than asking teams to assemble separate tools around a standalone physics engine.


Cofounders Matei Gardea and Daniel Grant met during their master’s studies in electrical engineering and computer science at UC Berkeley. Their public YC profiles describe robotics-research experience, including Berkeley’s robotics community. Grant’s profile also lists research with the Oxford Robotics Institute, Google DeepMind and NASA’s Advanced Supercomputing Division.


The company is part of YC’s Fall 2026 batch and is seeking discussions with teams working on robot foundation models, training and evaluation. The materials reviewed do not disclose pricing, a customer list or a general-availability date for Horizon. The launch presents a platform being built and the workflows it aims to support.


The underlying bet is that better simulation can expand experimentation without requiring every additional test to happen on a physical robot. For potential users, the decisive evidence will be how the simulator handles their particular manipulation tasks and how those results transfer. Outworld’s announcement explains the direction, while leaving those performance questions to future validation.
